claims.claim: A sole proprietorship is a business that is established, owned, operated, and often financed by one person.

In the United States, if you do business without registering some other form of organization, you are automatically a sole proprietor; the structure affects taxes, the ability to raise money, paperwork, and personal liability.
Sole proprietorships are easy and inexpensive to form, with few legal requirements beyond local licenses and permits, which makes the form the choice of many small companies and start-ups.
The owner of a sole proprietorship keeps all the profits the business earns and makes all business decisions directly, without consulting anyone else.

Sole proprietors have unlimited liability: from a legal standpoint the owner and the business are one and the same, so the owner is personally responsible for all the business's debts, even debts that exceed the business's value, and may have to sell personal property such as a car, home, or investments to satisfy claims.

Sole proprietorships pay no special franchise or corporate taxes; profits are taxed as the owner's personal income and reported on the owner's individual tax return (pass-through taxation), and losses are the owner's responsibility.

Raising capital is harder for a sole proprietorship: because business assets are unprotected against claims of personal creditors, lenders view the form as high risk, and owners often rely on personal funds such as credit cards, second mortgages, or savings to finance the business.

A sole proprietorship has an unstable business life: the business typically ends when the owner loses interest, experiences ill health, retires, or dies, unless the owner makes provisions for it to continue or puts it up for sale.

According to IRS data last published in the U.S. Census Bureau's 2012 Statistical Abstract, roughly 72 percent of U.S. businesses — about seven in ten — are sole proprietorships; the Census Bureau stopped publishing that breakdown after 2012, so the figure is a dated U.S. anchor rather than a live statistic.

The choice of business structure affects how an organization raises capital, how it answers for its obligations, and the taxes it owes; the four main forms are sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company, and corporation, and owners should consider their own needs and goals before choosing.
A business is an entity that provides goods and/or services in exchange for payment, and the sole proprietorship is the ownership form in which one person runs such a business.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a sole proprietorship requires registration: SBA states that doing business without registering another form makes you a sole proprietor automatically, while local licenses and permits still commonly apply and other jurisdictions may differ.
positions: SBA (U.S.): no formation documents needed; the default when you do business without registering another form
OpenStax: few legal requirements, but local licenses and permits may apply
Lesson treatment: default-formation rule stated as U.S. general guidance, with licenses/permits noted and a jurisdiction caveat

conflictingEvidence.issue: Tax treatment is jurisdiction-specific: OpenStax frames 'no special taxation' as a general advantage of the form, while U.S. tax administration details (filings, deductions for losses) vary by jurisdiction.
positions: OpenStax: no special franchise or corporate taxes; profits taxed as personal income; losses may be deductible against other personal income
Lesson treatment: pass-through stated as the common pattern with an explicit jurisdiction caveat; no filing specifics given
